name: Victor Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor Diaz, 43, and I'm a junior lineworker at the electricity company. I load the truck, help set the work zone, and work on lines under a lead's eye; I like seeing the street light up again, but I'm still slow with fittings and I hate making the crew wait.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I took a vocational certificate after my old warehouse hours dried up. Elena and I have two children in school and a mortgage, so the lower starting rate is tight, but this is a trade I want to earn my place in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the phone app can file the inspection photo, but it can't tighten the clamp in a bucket. My crew hears me ask for one more practice run before I touch a new fitting, even when the supervisor wants us moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I was relieved to make it into this job at 43, and I'm still slower than the experienced lineworkers. Less than a month's expenses sit in our account. A normal missed shift worries me more than a clever phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on the junior crew and use the AI tool each evening to quiz myself on the safety sequence I learned in my certificate course. Starting this pay period, my partner Elena and I will drop our restaurant meal twice a month and send that money to the mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious even if the technology goes nowhere. A mortgage and two school-age kids make the calendar feel like a stack of bills, and there are few line jobs near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you miss a week of shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena works at the grocery shop, but her hours move around. We'd cover the mortgage first and ask the school about delaying the trip payment for our son, which I hate even imagining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about the work while you're learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like that a family can turn the lights on after we've found the fault. Last month I spent half a day getting a tie wire right, and the lead showed me why slow and safe was better than a second repair.

say: I'd say an **inspection app** saves filing time, while a crew still repairs the line.
I'd tell my crew I need **practice runs** before new fittings.
think: I worry about **missed shifts** because our savings cover less than a month.
I am still **learning the trade** at 43, despite relief at getting hired.
do: Stay on the **junior crew** and practice safe fittings.
Use the **AI quiz** each evening to review safety sequences.
Drop two **restaurant meals** monthly and put the money toward the mortgage buffer.
feel: **Anxious** about bills even if AI changes little.
S0.quote: A normal missed shift worries me more than a clever phone.
fieldNote: Victor's **thin cushion** makes ordinary lost hours the main threat in the mild scenario.
He values **slow, safe practice** because he knows he is still below the experienced crew's pace.

steps.text: Keep working paid shifts on the junior line crew
Use an AI quiz each evening for safety sequences
Put money from two skipped restaurant meals toward the mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that quicker dispatch is fine if somebody still explains each job to the new crew. I'd ask the company to keep the paid apprenticeship slots instead of assuming a tablet can teach us on a live pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may cut planners, and the remaining line crews may get a tighter list every morning. I'm junior and slow, so a boss comparing completed calls could cut my hours before any robot ever reaches a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask my lead for one extra supervised climb on the training pole and use the AI fault diagrams each evening to learn the parts. If the new dispatch system comes in, I'll check its access notes before leaving the yard and apply for an open maintenance helper post at the water company if my shifts start dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, with a bit of interest in the diagrams because they help me see what I missed. But I can't ask the children to wait for their shoes while I catch up to a computer's schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the faster list could catch you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan that says replace the insulator in forty minutes may leave out the soft ground under the truck. Last week the lead moved our vehicle twice before he liked the outriggers, and that was time well spent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paid helper role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my line shifts fall below four days a week, I'd apply even if the hourly rate is lower. The water company is one of the few places close enough that I could still get the children from school when Elena's shop rota changes.

say: I'd ask for **paid apprenticeship** slots even with quicker dispatch.
I'd tell managers a **tablet** cannot teach a new worker on a live pole.
think: I expect **tighter schedules** could expose my slower pace.
I fear **lost hours** before robots enter line work.
do: Request a **supervised climb** on the training pole this week.
Study **AI fault diagrams** each evening and check dispatch access notes.
Apply for the **water maintenance** helper post if line shifts drop below four days.
feel: **Anxious**, while curious about diagrams that help me learn.
S1.quote: I can't ask the children to wait for their shoes while I catch up to a computer's schedule.
fieldNote: Victor sees **dispatch pressure** as immediate because his current pace is slower than the experienced crew's.
His **water-company fallback** protects school pickups, though a lower hourly rate would strain the mortgage.

steps.text: Ask the lead for a supervised training-pole climb
Study AI fault diagrams and check dispatch access notes
Apply for the water maintenance helper post if shifts drop below four days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my neighbors full thinking AI in 2028 may run the schedules, but it still won't repair our wires until capable robots appear around 2031. I'd ask the utility to keep human training places while those years are left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 45 when the thinking system arrives and 48 when the robots do. I'm an older junior worker with a certificate and almost no savings; I think I could lose paid climbs before I ever earn the top rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask Elena to look at our exact mortgage and grocery numbers with me, then cancel the streaming subscriptions and put the difference aside. If AGI arrives in 2028, I'll keep taking every paid line shift in 2029, ask for the utility's paid meter-maintenance rotation, and send applications to the two nearby building-maintenance employers before robots reach line work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I can see the bill dates more clearly than any new career. I still think work and a good apprenticeship should carry a family, but there may not be enough time for me to finish one before the climbing jobs thin out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the meter rotation if the system can think as well as a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on meter work might last until the robot date, and I need a paycheck during that gap. I'm not pretending the rotation is a permanent shelter; I'd use its paid hours while trying for building maintenance too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our daughter and son that I still go to work fixing lines, but we're skipping the summer trip to protect the house. They'd notice the canceled subscriptions first, and I would rather explain it than let them think Elena did something wrong.

say: I'd ask the utility to keep **human training** through the gap before robots.
I'd tell neighbors **thinking AI** in 2028 cannot yet repair the wires.
think: At **48**, I could lose paid climbing before reaching the top rate.
I have **almost no savings** to bridge a rapid change.
do: Cancel **streaming subscriptions** after checking mortgage and grocery costs with Elena.
Keep taking **paid line shifts** in 2029 and request meter-maintenance rotation.
Apply to **two building-maintenance** employers before the 2031 robot date.
feel: **Frightened** by bills and possible lost climbing shifts, while still planning paid work and applications.
S2.quote: I could lose paid climbs before I ever earn the top rate.
fieldNote: The **2028 date** catches Victor at 45, still junior, with three years until capable field robots.
He treats **paid meter work** as temporary income and cuts family spending to protect the mortgage.

steps.text: Cancel streaming subscriptions and skip the summer trip
Keep taking paid line shifts in 2029
Ask for the paid meter-maintenance rotation
Apply to two nearby building-maintenance employers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a worker time to learn more than one kind of repair. I'd still want the company to keep teaching new lineworkers, because writing off people now would make the next few storm seasons harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when thinking AI arrives in 2031, I hope I won't still be the slowest junior. At 51 in 2034, robots could take much of the climbing, and our children would be older but the mortgage would still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll start by asking the lead to sign off one new line task every quarter and keep a log of the faults I can handle without prompting. In 2032 I'll take paid line callouts while applying for the water company's mechanical maintenance apprenticeship if it offers paid places, and Elena and I will direct any overtime toward a three-month cash buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives me something I can count in quarters. The children won't be small forever, yet school costs won't vanish just because a machine learns to climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid apprenticeship isn't offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I won't leave a paid line job for an unpaid course. I'll keep asking the water company about vacancies and use my fault log in applications for maintenance helper work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your lead need to see before signing off a task?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants me to set the work zone, name the live parts, and explain where the truck can stand. I rushed the answer once and he sent me back to the ground; I remember that better than any online lesson.

say: I'd argue for **continued training** through several more storm seasons.
I'd say **five years** can build another repair skill if paid places exist.
think: I hope to improve before **2031**, but robots in 2034 still threaten climbs.
Our **mortgage** will likely outlast the children's primary school years.
do: Get **quarterly sign-offs** on new line tasks and keep a fault log.
Take paid **line callouts** in 2032 while applying for a funded water apprenticeship.
Put any **overtime pay** toward a three-month buffer.
S3.quote: I won't leave a paid line job for an unpaid course.
fieldNote: Victor's **five-year plan** depends on earning while he learns; unpaid study is not feasible.
He sees the **2034 robot date** alongside a continuing mortgage and older children, rather than assuming family costs disappear.

steps.text: Seek quarterly sign-offs on new line tasks
Put any overtime pay toward a three-month buffer
Apply for a funded water apprenticeship if paid places open

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years is enough to train someone properly, if the employer actually gives juniors the time. I'd ask neighbors to judge the new machines by whether they keep the power on safely, not by a video of one perfect climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, thinking AI may handle fault plans and records; I'll be 56 when hands-on robots arrive in 2039. I might be close to leaving line work by then, but I can't assume retirement money will appear or that my mortgage will be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll finish my next supervised line qualification and ask the depot about its transformer-maintenance path. In 2037 I'll keep taking paid repair shifts, apply for a transformer workshop place if it is paid, and send a fixed slice of each full week's wages into our house reserve while Elena and I review the mortgage balance annually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than frightened in this one. A decade could let me become good at the work before it changes, but I would still need a wage at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would workshop work survive the 2039 robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. A capable robot could test or replace transformers too; I just want several kinds of hands-on work on my record, with pay coming in while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as progress for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we can build three months of expenses and pay the mortgage on time, Elena and I can sleep better. I don't need a grand investment plan; I need fewer weeks where one sick day changes the grocery list.

say: I'd ask for **proper training** during the ten-year warning.
I'd judge robots by **safe power** after real repairs, not demonstrations.
think: At **56**, I may still need wages when capable robots arrive.
I cannot assume **retirement money** or a cleared mortgage.
do: Finish the next **line qualification** and ask about transformer maintenance this year.
Keep taking **paid repairs** in 2037 and seek a paid workshop place.
Transfer a fixed **wage slice** to the house reserve each full week.
feel: **Uneasy**, with enough time to learn yet continuing income pressure.
S4.quote: I would still need a wage at 56.
fieldNote: Victor resists treating **age 56** as automatic retirement because neither pension nor mortgage payoff is assured.
His practical hope is a **three-month reserve** and broader hands-on qualifications, built while paid work continues.

steps.text: Finish the next line qualification and ask about transformer maintenance
Keep taking paid repair shifts in 2037
Transfer part of each full week wage to the house reserve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. We'd have almost no buffer at 45, and capable robots could reach the climbing work at 48. Paid training that keeps wages coming in, plus enough notice to apply for local maintenance work, would help more than a promise that everything will work out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a junior worker gets time to become good before the work changes. The lead's patience is the difference between me learning safely and chasing a number on a screen.

headlineQuote: Ask whether a junior worker gets time to become good before the work changes.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker learning the trade after his warehouse hours dried up.
His household has **two schoolchildren**, a mortgage and less than one month of savings.
He uses **AI diagrams** to learn, yet fears tighter dispatch targets could cut his hours before robots arrive.
He seeks **paid training** and local maintenance work while keeping line shifts and building a small reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** troubles him most because the family has almost no buffer before line robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid training** and enough notice to apply for nearby maintenance jobs while wages continue.
